grammar.title: Sretan and sretna greetings
grammar.explanation: Sretan pairs with masculine holiday names such as Bajram and Božić. Sretna pairs with feminine phrases such as Nova godina. Learn each full greeting as one line you can reuse.

grammar.title: Čestitam plus the holiday
grammar.explanation: Čestitam plus the holiday name is a warm way to offer congratulations. Keep the present form and let your voice do the smiling. It works across different communities.

grammar.title: Inclusive holiday talk
grammar.explanation: Name more than one holiday so your greetings stay inclusive. Add zajedno when people celebrate side by side on the same street. Present-tense wishes are enough for market conversations.

culture.title: Lights, markets, and shared greetings
culture.body: Holiday lights on Ferhadija turn central Sarajevo into a shared evening walk for many neighbors. Nearby, Gazi Husrev-beg's Mosque and the Sacred Heart Cathedral stand as reminders that different communities mark the calendar in their own ways. Ana practices Sretan Bajram, Sretan Božić, and Sretna Nova godina, all with equal warmth. A market stall sells čestitke while svjetla glitter above the crowd and music spills from the cafés. Greeting more than one holiday keeps friendship open through the season and makes the street feel a little wider. One well-chosen wish goes further than a flawless grammar explanation.

lessonBlocks.title: Lesson A. Three holiday wishes
lessonBlocks.body: Learn the three core wishes first: Sretan Bajram, Sretan Božić, and Sretna Nova godina. Notice sretan versus sretna, and keep each greeting whole as one spoken line. Add Čestitam Bajram as a second warm pattern you can offer family or friends. Ana repeats the greetings while Emir points to mosque and cathedral photos on the same city map. This is about speaking respectfully in public, not giving a lecture on religion or drawing comparisons between faiths. Practice each wish a couple of times, then switch which holiday you greet so your mouth stays flexible. Keep the tone warm and each greeting complete.
tips: Memorize each full greeting as one line.
Watch sretan versus sretna before you speak.
Practice all three so you can answer different neighbors.

lessonBlocks.title: Lesson B. Market politeness and cards
lessonBlocks.body: Take the greetings into a market scene with svjetla, dar, and čestitka in your pocket vocabulary. Say Molim and Hvala at the stall, then wish the seller a holiday that fits the moment. Amira likes the Nova godina lights, Emir talks about Bajram visits, and Ana sends a Božić card to family abroad. Practice switching greetings so you can answer whoever you meet on Ferhadija after dark. End with Slavimo zajedno, a friendly present-tense line that leaves room for everyone's calendar. A card plus a spoken wish is often enough to make the season feel shared. Try writing one card message before you leave the stall.
tips: Use molim and hvala at the market stall.
Hand over a čestitka with a spoken wish.
Say Slavimo zajedno when the mood is shared.

funFacts.title: Ferhadija is a holiday promenade
funFacts.body: Ferhadija Street fills with evening walkers when lights go up for winter seasons. Shops, cafés, and market noise make greetings feel natural in the middle of it all. The foot traffic is part of the city's social rhythm. Practicing wishes here feels lived-in rather than staged.

funFacts.title: Two landmarks, one center
funFacts.body: Gazi Husrev-beg's Mosque and the Sacred Heart Cathedral stand close together in downtown Sarajevo. Their nearness is a reminder that more than one holiday calendar shapes public life here. Photos of both places help you picture more than a single community. Respect starts with naming things accurately.

funFacts.title: Čestitka carries a written wish
funFacts.body: A čestitka is a greeting card you can hand over along with a spoken line. Writing Sretan Bajram or Sretan Božić helps the phrase stick. Small gifts and cards keep contact warm across distance. Holding the object in your hands makes the phrase easier to remember.

civicContext.title: Gulf money rebuilt mosques and shifted teaching
civicContext.body: Holiday lights on Ferhadija look shared, yet some prayer spaces were rebuilt with money that came attached to its own agenda. After the war, destroyed mosques rose again with large Gulf donations. Sarajevo's King Fahd Mosque is a clear Saudi-funded example. Some of that funding also supported more conservative teaching than older Bosnian Islamic practice had. Inclusive market greetings sit beside rebuilt pulpits where outside money changed who teaches and how.
